title: Build your own vtable
description:
C has no virtual functions, so C programs (and the Windows COM system) build vtables by hand. Do the same, to see there is no magic.

A `Shape` holds a pointer to a `ShapeVTable` (its "vptr") and two numbers. The table holds two function pointers: `area` and `name`. Write:

- `circleArea`, `rectArea`: compute the area from the shape's numbers. A circle uses `a` as its radius (use 3.14159265358979 for pi); a rectangle uses `a` and `b` as width and height.
- `circleName`, `rectName`: return `"circle"` and `"rectangle"`.
- the two tables `kCircleTable` and `kRectTable`, filled with the right functions;
- `makeCircle(r)` and `makeRect(w, h)`, which return a `Shape` aimed at the right table;
- `totalArea(shapes)`, which adds up the areas **by calling through each shape's table**.
hints: Fill each table with the addresses of its two functions, in the order the struct declares them: `{ &circleArea, &circleName }`.
`makeCircle` must set `vptr` to `&kCircleTable`. Every circle points at the same table.
In `totalArea`, call `s.vptr->area(s)`. Do not check what kind of shape it is: the table decides.
lessonTitle: Virtual Functions and Vtables in Memory
